title: The captive dependency trap (scoped inside singleton)
hook: When a singleton holds a reference to a scoped service, the scoped instance lives as long as the singleton — not one request. This captive dependency anti-pattern causes stale data, thread-safety violations, and memory leaks.

blocks.text: The captive dependency trap occurs when a longer-lived service (singleton) captures a shorter-lived service (scoped or transient) in its constructor. The container resolves the scoped service once at singleton creation time and stores the reference forever. In ASP.NET Core, common victims are DbContext, per-request tenant contexts, and IMemoryCache entries tied to a request. The scoped service never gets disposed at request end because the singleton prevents the scope from releasing it.

entries.plainDefinition: A longer-lived object holds a reference to a shorter-lived dependency, extending its lifetime incorrectly.
entries.example: Singleton CacheWarmer injecting scoped AppDbContext in constructor

entries.example: Resolving scoped service from root without CreateScope() is invalid

blocks.text: This is the most common DI interview trap and a top production bug on Reddit r/dotnet. Symptoms appear only under concurrency: random wrong tenant data, ObjectDisposedException, growing memory from undisposed DbContext instances, and corrupted EF change trackers. Locally with one request it works fine — which is why ValidateOnBuild in CI is critical.

blocks.title: Real production symptom
blocks.body: Under load, API returns data from another user's request. Root cause: singleton service captured scoped TenantContext at startup. One tenant ID forever.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: How a scoped service gets captured

items.title: Singleton created at startup
items.body: Container constructs the singleton, resolving all constructor dependencies.

items.title: Scoped resolved from root
items.body: Without an active scope, the container may still resolve scoped (if ValidateScopes is off) — one instance created.

items.title: Reference stored forever
items.body: The singleton holds the scoped instance in a private field for the app lifetime.

items.title: Concurrent requests share it
items.body: All requests use the same DbContext/tenant — thread-safety violations and data leaks.

diagram.title: Captive dependency lifecycle
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as Application Startup
  participant S as Singleton Service
  participant DB as Scoped DbContext
  participant R1 as Request 1
  participant R2 as Request 2
  App->>S: new SingletonService(db)
  App->>DB: resolve once (captive)
  S->>DB: stores reference
  R1->>S: uses shared DB
  R2->>S: uses SAME DB
  Note over DB: Never disposed per request

snippet.label: WRONG — singleton capturing scoped DbContext
snippet.explanation: IHostedService is singleton. Injecting AppDbContext captures one context forever. Concurrent StartAsync and later requests share it — not thread-safe.

snippet.label: CORRECT — IServiceScopeFactory for scoped work in singleton
snippet.explanation: CreateScope() creates a short-lived scope. DbContext is resolved within that scope and disposed when the using block ends. This is the fix for any singleton needing scoped services.

snippet.label: ValidateOnBuild catches captive dependencies at startup
snippet.explanation: With validation enabled, the app fails at Build() — not at 3 AM under concurrent load. Always enable ValidateOnBuild in CI pipelines.

snippet.label: Failure mode — concurrent requests on captive DbContext
snippet.explanation: This diagnostics snippet documents the exact exception messages and counter to watch. ActiveDbContexts stuck at 1 under concurrent load proves captive dependency.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Disabling ValidateScopes in production to ship faster. Storing scoped service in a singleton's field during a method call for 'later use'. Injecting scoped into middleware constructor (middleware is singleton). Using BuildServiceProvider() in a singleton and never disposing the scope.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters monitor Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore — active-db-contexts stuck at 1 under 50 concurrent requests is definitive proof. Application Insights exceptions containing 'second operation on this context'. Parallel integration test with WebApplicationFactory asserting tenant isolation. Code review automation: Roslyn analyzer or grep for scoped types in singleton constructors. ValidateOnBuild in every CI pipeline — zero cost at runtime, catches 90% of captive bugs pre-deploy.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Only direct ctor injection — not runtime field assignment

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Not knowing what captive dependency means. Saying 'it works on my machine' without explaining concurrency. Unable to name ValidateOnBuild or IServiceScopeFactory as fixes. Claiming transient in singleton ctor is safe — transient is also captured and never recreated.

interviewTakeaways: Captive dependency: singleton holds scoped/transient reference — scoped lives forever, not per request.
ValidateOnBuild + ValidateScopes in CI catch this at startup; never disable ValidateScopes to ship.
Production tip: dotnet-counters active-db-contexts ≈ concurrent requests; stuck at 1 = captive DbContext.

60s: Singleton ctor resolving scoped DbContext captures one instance for app lifetime. Concurrent requests share it — not thread-safe, cross-tenant leaks. Fix: IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope(). ValidateOnBuild fails at startup.
Follow-up: does injecting transient into singleton have the same problem?
commonPitfalls: Saying transient in singleton ctor is fine gets you rejected — transient is also captured once, never recreated per call.
Disabling ValidateScopes in production — the #1 reason captive bugs reach prod.
Strong answer: 'Longer lifetime cannot hold shorter. Singleton + scoped DbContext = captive. Fix with IServiceScopeFactory. ValidateOnBuild in CI. NestJS has same rule with REQUEST in DEFAULT scope.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 1.0 DI; ValidateScopes in 2.0; ValidateOnBuild in generic host

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS throws at bootstrap if a singleton provider injects a REQUEST-scoped provider — identical validation to ValidateScopes. The fix is ModuleRef.resolve() or restructuring to handler-level injection.
